derivations.claim: If $K=0$, every entry is zero almost surely and the conclusion is immediate. Assume $K>0$. Regard the complex unit sphere in $\mathbb C^d$ as the real unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{2d}$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, a maximal $\varepsilon$-separated subset is an $\varepsilon$-net; the disjoint radius-$\varepsilon/2$ balls about its points lie in the radius-$(1+\varepsilon/2)$ ball, so volume comparison bounds its cardinality by $(1+2/\varepsilon)^{2d}$. If $\mathcal N_1,\mathcal N_2$ are such nets for the two unit spheres and $A$ is an $n\times N$ complex matrix, approximating unit vectors $u,v$ attaining $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|u^*Av|$ gives $$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le (1-2\varepsilon)^{-1}\max_{u_0\in\mathcal N_1,\ v_0\in\mathcal N_2}|u_0^*Av_0|.$$ Indeed, the approximation error is at most $\|u-u_0\|\|A\|+\|v-v_0\|\|A\|\le2\varepsilon\|A\|$.

Fix deterministic unit vectors $u\in\mathbb C^n$ and $v\in\mathbb C^N$. Then $u^*X_nv=\sum_{i,j}\overline u_i v_j\xi_{ij}$ is a sum of independent centered complex variables. Each real or imaginary summand is bounded in absolute value by $K|u_i||v_j|$. If a centered real variable $Y$ is bounded by $b$, convexity of the exponential on $[-b,b]$ and $\mathbb EY=0$ give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le\cosh(\lambda b)\le e^{\lambda^2b^2/2}$. Independence, exponential Markov inequality [F3], and optimization in $\lambda$ therefore give $$\mathbb P\{|u^*X_nv|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{4K^2}\right),$$ because $\sum_{i,j}K^2|u_i|^2|v_j|^2=K^2$.

Choose $\varepsilon=1/8$ in step 1.1. The product of the two net cardinalities is at most $17^{2(n+N_n)}$. Taking $t=L\sqrt{n+N_n}$ with $L$ large enough that $L^2/(4K^2)>2\log17+1$, the union bound and step 2.1 make the probability that the net maximum exceeds $t$ at most $4e^{-(n+N_n)}$. These probabilities are summable in $n$ because $N_n/n\to1/c>0$. By [F2], the net maximum is at most $L\sqrt{n+N_n}$ eventually almost surely. The net inequality in step 1.1 and boundedness of $n/N_n$ then yield $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually, with deterministic $C=C(K,c)$. Since all $X_n$ are defined on the common probability space in the Statement, [F2] applies to this sequence of events.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For positive integers $d,N$, let $X\in\mathbb C^{d\times N}$ and let $T\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, meaning $T=T^*$ and $v^*Tv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^d$. Let $T^{1/2}$ be its Hermitian positive semidefinite square root and set
$$A:=\frac1N T^{1/2}XX^*T^{1/2}.$$
For each distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$ of the Hermitian matrix $A$, let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto its eigenspace. The empirical spectral distribution of $A$, normalized by its dimension $d$, is
$$\mu_A:=\frac1d\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)\,\delta_\lambda,$$
where $\delta_\lambda$ is the unit point mass at $\lambda$.
For a deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure is
$$\mu_A^x:=\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\,\delta_\lambda.$$
For a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, set $\mathbf1_B(A):=\sum_{\lambda\in B\cap\operatorname{spec}(A)}P_\lambda$; then $\mu_A^x(B)=x^*\mathbf1_B(A)x$. Both measures are supported on the nonnegative real axis.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, second absolute moment one and $|X_{ij}|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K$, and let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite (self-adjoint with $v^*T_nv\ge0$ for every $v$) with induced Euclidean operator norm $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$. Define
$$A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n,$$
$$R_n(z)=(A_n-zI_n)^{-1},\qquad \widetilde R_n(z)=(\widetilde A_n-zI_{N_n})^{-1},\qquad q_n(z)=\mathbb E\left[N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\widetilde R_n(z)\right].$$
For every fixed $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, the matrix $I_n+q_n(z)T_n$ is invertible and
$$\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\left|x^*\left(\mathbb E R_n(z)+\frac1z(I_n+q_n(z)T_n)^{-1}\right)x\right|\longrightarrow0.$$

On a common probability space, for each positive integer $n$, let $Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,N_n}$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb C^n$, let $B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^*$, and assume $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, and define
$$M_n(z):=\frac1n\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2n^2\eta^2}{4N_n}\right),$$
and $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$ almost surely.

Let $c>0$, let $H$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,\infty)$, and fix $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. There is at most one $q\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}q>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$q=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czq)-z}\,dH(t).$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, with Stieltjes transform $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. For every $a<b$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mu((a,b))+\tfrac12\mu(\{a\})+\tfrac12\mu(\{b\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du,\qquad \mu(\{x\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta\,\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta).$$
If two Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ have the same Stieltjes transform on the upper half-plane, then they are equal.

On a common probability space, for each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have independent identically distributed entries $\xi$ satisfying $\mathbb E\xi=0$ and $|\xi|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K<\infty$. Then there is a finite constant $C=C(K,c)$ such that, almost surely, $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{N_n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For Hermitian $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, write their eigenvalues in
descending order with multiplicity as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(A)$
and $\lambda_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(B)$. Then, for every $j$,
$$|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|_2.$$

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Write $c_n=n/N_n$, let $\bar F_n(B)=\mathbb E F_n(B)$, and let $\bar G_n$ be defined similarly for $\widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n$. By [F14], each ordered eigenvalue is continuous in the matrix entries, so these setwise expectations are defined for Borel $B$. For disjoint Borel sets, countable additivity of the random ESDs followed by [F13] gives countable additivity of $\bar F_n$ and $\bar G_n$; their total masses are one. Independence and unit second moment give $\int t\,d\bar F_n(t)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$ and $\int t\,d\bar G_n(t)=N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$. Both first moments are uniformly bounded because $c_n\to c>0$ and $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is uniformly bounded. By [F4], their tails above $R$ are at most the corresponding first moment divided by $R$, so both expected-measure sequences are tight on $[0,\infty)$. The half-line is Polish: it is a closed subset of the complete real line and $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$ is dense. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence of $\bar F_n$ has a further weakly convergent subsequence.

For each fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$, [F7] gives $\int(t-z)^{-1}dF_n(t)-\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar F_n(t)\to0$ almost surely. Intersect these probability-one events over the countable dense set $\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ b>0\}$. All $X_n$ are on the common probability space in the Statement, so these events form one sequence.

Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and take any such subsequence with $\bar F_n\Rightarrow G$. Let $m_G(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}dG(t)$ and $q_n(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar G_n(t)$. The argument applies to every $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and every weak subsequential limit $G$. By [F8], all such limits have the same transform; [F9] makes them equal. At least one such limit exists by step 1.1, so call it $F_{c,H}$. Tightness then implies $\bar F_n\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$.

On the same event, [F10] gives $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_1$ eventually for a finite deterministic $L_1$, so the random measures $F_n$ are eventually supported on $[0,L_1]$ and are tight. The half-line is Polish by the metric facts in step 1.1 and [F15]. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes and
In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix.

Let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ be any finite real or complex matrix, and let $M^\dagger$ be its unique Moore-Penrose inverse. Then $P=MM^\dagger$ and $Q=M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint idempotents. The range of $P$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$, and the range of $Q$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$. Thus both are orthogonal projections. If $M$ has full row rank, then $MM^\dagger=I_p$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let all the matrices $X_n$ be defined on one common probability space. For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\mu_n$ be its empirical spectral distribution normalized by $p_n$. Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly almost surely to the probability measure with density

$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single

$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

On a common probability space, for each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, unit second absolute moment, and absolute value at most $K$, where $K$ is independent of $n$. $$\mathbb P\!\left\{|x_n^*R_n(z)x_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_n(z)x_n]|>t\right\}\le\frac{C}{t^4N_n^2}.$$

The Penrose equation $X_nX_n^+X_n=X_n$ shows $\ker(P_n)=\ker(X_n)$: if $X_nv=0$, then $P_nv=0$, and if $P_nv=0$, then $X_nv=X_nX_n^+X_nv=X_nP_nv=0$. Conditional on $X_n$, the cross term has expectation zero because $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_n\mid X_n]=0$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of complex random variables with $\mathbb E\xi_{11}=0$, $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^2=1$, and $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be positive with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$ and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le N_n}$ be its upper-left block. Let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite with uniformly bounded operator norm and empirical eigenvalue measures $H_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{\lambda_i(T_n)}\Rightarrow H$. Let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic unit vectors such that, for every $w\in\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$,
$$x_n^*(T_n-wI_n)^{-1}x_n\longrightarrow m_H(w):=\int_{[0,\infty)}(t-w)^{-1}\,dH(t).$$
Define $A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2}$ and $\mu_n^{x_n}(B)=x_n^*\mathbf1_B(A_n)x_n$ for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$. Then almost surely $\mu_n^{x_n}$ converges weakly to the probability measure $F_{c,H}$ whose Stieltjes transform is the unique $m\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}m>0$, $u=-(1-c)/z+cm$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$m=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czm)-z}\,dH(t),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

Under the hypotheses of the sample-covariance resolvent deterministic-equivalent theorem, for each fixed $s>0$ the directional measures satisfy
$$\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t+s}\,d\mu_n^{x_n}(t)\longrightarrow\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t+s}\,dF_{c,H}(t)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

For positive integers $d,N$, let $X\in\mathbb C^{d\times N}$ and let $T\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, meaning $T=T^*$ and $v^*Tv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^d$. Let $T^{1/2}$ be its Hermitian positive semidefinite square root and set
$$A:=\frac1N T^{1/2}XX^*T^{1/2}.$$
For each distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$ of the Hermitian matrix $A$, let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto its eigenspace. The empirical spectral distribution of $A$, normalized by its dimension $d$, is
$$\mu_A:=\frac1d\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)\,\delta_\lambda,$$
where $\delta_\lambda$ is the unit point mass at $\lambda$.
For a deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure is
$$\mu_A^x:=\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\,\delta_\lambda.$$
For a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, set $\mathbf1_B(A):=\sum_{\lambda\in B\cap\operatorname{spec}(A)}P_\lambda$; then $\mu_A^x(B)=x^*\mathbf1_B(A)x$. Both measures are supported on the nonnegative real axis.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $c>0$, let $H$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,\infty)$, and fix $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. There is at most one $q\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}q>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$q=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czq)-z}\,dH(t).$$

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, with Stieltjes transform $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. For every $a<b$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mu((a,b))+\tfrac12\mu(\{a\})+\tfrac12\mu(\{b\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du,\qquad \mu(\{x\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta\,\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta).$$
If two Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ have the same Stieltjes transform on the upper half-plane, then they are equal.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ (Sigma-algebras) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Work on the probability-one weak-convergence event of step 1.1. For each integer $j\ge1$, set $b_j=2^{-j}$ and $a_j=b_j/2$, and define the bounded continuous real function $\varphi_j(t)=\max\{0,1-|2t-a_j-b_j|/(b_j-a_j)\}$ on $\mathbb R$. On $(a_j,b_j)$, [F3] gives $\rho_1(t)\ge\sqrt{4-b_j}/(2\pi\sqrt{b_j})>0$. Applying the order and scalar rules in [F8] first to $\varphi_j\ge\tfrac12\mathbf1_{J_j}$ under $\mu_1$, then to this density lower bound on $J_j$ under Lebesgue measure, gives $\int\varphi_j\,d\mu_1\ge\tfrac12\mu_1(J_j)\ge(b_j-a_j)\sqrt{4-b_j}/(8\pi\sqrt{b_j})>0$, since $J_j$ has length $(b_j-a_j)/2$. By [F4] and step 1.1, $\int\varphi_j\,d\mu_n^{x_n}\to\int\varphi_j\,d\mu_1$, so for each $j$ this sample integral is eventually positive. Since $0\le\varphi_j\le\mathbf1_{(a_j,b_j)}$, [F8] gives $0<\int\varphi_j\,d\mu_n^{x_n}\le\mu_n^{x_n}((a_j,b_j))$. The finite atomic set formula in [F4] makes the right side $\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A_n)\cap(a_j,b_j)}\|P_\lambda x_n\|_2^2$; therefore there is an actual eigenvalue in $(a_j,b_j)$.

These conclusions hold for all $j$ on the same weak-convergence event, since its bounded-continuous-test property applies to each $\varphi_j$.
